sections.overview: The domestic cat is a small carnivorous mammal descended chiefly from Near Eastern wildcats. Its association with people began around early farming settlements, where rodents gathered near stored grain. Cats spread widely with human travel while retaining much of their ancestral hunting behaviour.
sections.identification: A compact, four-legged feline, it has a flexible spine, padded feet, sensitive whiskers and retractile claws. Coat length, colour, pattern, body size and tail shape vary widely among individuals and breeds; most cats nevertheless share a broadly similar, agile build. The consulted species account gives a typical adult length of about 76 cm and a mass of 4.1–5.4 kg; males are generally larger, while breed and body condition create substantial variation.
sections.habitat: Cats now occur worldwide, especially around settlements. They live in homes, farms, towns and suburbs, while unowned or free-roaming populations often remain near present or former human habitation. Shelter, food supplied by people and access to small prey influence where they settle.
sections.diet: Cats are obligate meat-eaters. They stalk and ambush small prey, commonly rodents and birds, and may also catch reptiles, insects or fish. A free-roaming cat can hunt even when people provide food, so hunting is not simply a response to hunger.
sections.behavior: Hunting combines quiet approach, a sudden pounce and a bite; play rehearses parts of this sequence. Cats communicate through posture, sound, touch and scent marks. Though often solitary and territorial, they can form social groups where food and shelter are concentrated.
sections.reproduction: Females can cycle repeatedly during a breeding season, with timing affected by daylight and conditions. Mating commonly induces ovulation; pregnancy lasts roughly two months. Kittens are born dependent, nursed by their mother, and gradually weaned over their first weeks; paternal care is uncommon.
sections.ecology: Free-ranging cats also kill native wildlife, and research documents predation across many regions and islands. The outcome varies with prey, habitat, cat density and human feeding; island species can be especially vulnerable.
sections.conservation: The species is widespread through human care, but introduced, free-ranging populations create local conservation problems where native prey lack defences against mammalian hunters. Such impacts concern particular ecosystems and do not describe every domestic cat.
